claim: Mafb transcription initiates in parallel with the end of neurogenesis, with expression evident in the basal to middle regions of the cochlea by E13.5.
source: In situ hybridization confirmed that Mafb transcription initiates in parallel with the end of neurogenesis, with expression evident in the basal to middle regions of the cochlea by E13.5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B and comparison with known timing of SGN neurogenesis.

claim: Mafb protein was not present in SGNs at E13.5.
source: Protein was not yet present at this stage (Figure 1C,C′).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C,C′.

claim: Mafb protein could be detected in SGNs in the basal and middle turns by E15.5.
source: Two days later, Mafb protein could be detected in SGNs in the basal and middle turns (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: By E16.5, Mafb protein was localized to SGN nuclei along the entire length of the cochlea.
source: by E16.5, Mafb protein was localized to SGN nuclei along the entire length of the cochlea (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: High levels of Mafb persisted during early postnatal stages.
source: High levels of Mafb persisted during early postnatal stages (Figure 1F,J)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 1F,J.

claim: Mafb protein level peaked at P6.
source: and peaked at P6 (Figure 1G,J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 1G,J.

claim: After P6, Mafb was gradually translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: Afterward, Mafb was gradually translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and only a few SGNs maintained strong nuclear expression by P10 (Figure 1H, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: After the onset of hearing, Mafb was present at low levels in the SGN cytoplasm.
source: After the onset of hearing, Mafb was still present at low levels in the SGN cytoplasm (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Mafb expression was limited to SGNs at all stages examined.
source: At all stages, Mafb expression was limited to SGNs, with no protein detected in VGNs (data not shown) or other cell types of the inner ear.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining observations throughout development.

claim: Mafb is expressed throughout auditory synaptogenesis, which begins around perinatal stages and lasts for the first two postnatal weeks, peaking around P6.
source: Hence, Mafb defines the SGN subset of inner ear neurons and is expressed throughout auditory synaptogenesis, which begins around perinatal stages and lasts for the first two postnatal weeks, peaking around P6 (Sobkowicz et al., 1982; Huang et al., 2012; Safieddine et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by temporal expression pattern of Mafb and cited literature on timing of synaptogenesis.

claim: The Mafbflox allele produces no Mafb protein after germline Cre-mediated recombination.
source: However, after germline Cre-mediated recombination, homozygotes produced no Mafb protein (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mafb null mutants generated from the Mafbflox line exhibit the same phenotypes as previously published null mutants.
source: and exhibited the same phenotypes as previously published null mutants (Figure 2D–F), which die perinatally with defective respiratory rhythmogenesis, renal dysgenesis, and cystic inner ears (Sadl et al., 2002; Blanchi et al., 2003; Choo et al., 2006; Moriguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2D-F and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The inner ear developed normally in Foxg1Cre/+;Mafbflox/GFP mutants.
source: In contrast to previously described Mafb mutants (Cordes and Barsh, 1994; Choo et al., 2006), the inner ear developed normally in Foxg1Cre/+;Mafbflox/GFP mutants (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Mafb does not play a direct role in inner ear morphogenesis.
source: Thus, Mafb does not play a direct role in inner ear morphogenesis, consistent with previous conclusions that the inner ear phenotype is secondary to hindbrain malformation (Choo et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from normal inner ear development in Foxg1Cre/+;Mafbflox/GFP mutants and cited literature.

claim: The neurite organization of SGNs was unaffected by the loss of Mafb in Foxg1Cre/+;Mafbflox/GFP mutants.
source: The neurite organization of SGNs was also unaffected by the loss of Mafb (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by neurofilament staining shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Foxg1Cre/+;Mafbflox/GFP mice died at birth.
source: Unfortunately, analysis of later functions was not possible as Foxg1Cre/+;Mafbflox/GFP mice died at birth, likely due to central apnea.
evidence: Observation of lethality in mutant mice.

claim: In MafbCKO animals, Mafb was significantly reduced at E16.5.
source: In Tg(Neurog1-Cre);Mafbflox/GFP mice (hereafter referred to as MafbCKO), Mafb was significantly reduced at E16.5 (data not shown)
evidence: Stated observation of reduced Mafb at E16.5.

claim: In MafbCKO animals, Mafb was nearly undetectable by P5.
source: and nearly undetectable by P5 (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: MafbCKO mice live through adulthood.
source: However, unlike Mafb null mutants, MafbCKO mice live through adulthood, permitting analysis of auditory circuit assembly and function.
evidence: Observation of survival in MafbCKO mice.

claim: Early stages of SGN development proceeded normally in MafbCKO animals.
source: As expected, early stages of SGN development proceeded normally in MafbCKO animals, with no obvious change in the organization of SGN processes (Figure 3J,K) or SGN density (Figure 3L–N).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3J-N.

claim: Mafb is not required for the initial production or differentiation of SGNs.
source: Taken together with results from the Foxg1-Cre driver, we conclude that Mafb is not required for the initial production or differentiation of SGNs.
evidence: Inferred from normal early SGN development in both Foxg1-Cre and Neurog1-Cre driven Mafb mutants.

claim: Mutant SGNs still contact IHCs in MafbCKO animals.
source: Ultrastructural analysis revealed that mutant SGNs still contact IHCs, indicating normal targeting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: GluR2 staining intensity was much lower in MafbCKO animals at P6 compared to controls.
source: In contrast, GluR2 staining intensity was much lower in MafbCKO animals (Figure 4B,K) (p<0.03), indicating that GluR2 fails to accumulate postsynaptically.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4B,K.

claim: MafbCKO ribbons were not paired with an obvious PSD even when in close contact with an afferent SGN terminal at P6.
source: In contrast, MafbCKO ribbons were not paired with an obvious PSD even when in close contact with an afferent SGN terminal (Figure 4E,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Anti-CtBP2 immunofluorescence intensity was noticeably reduced in MafbCKO mutants at P6.
source: In contrast, anti-CtBP2 immunofluorescence intensity was noticeably reduced in MafbCKO mutants at P6 (Figure 4B′), consistent with observation of small ribbons in electron micrographs (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B′ and electron microscopy in Figure 4F.

claim: Ribbon number was significantly decreased in MafbCKO mutants at P6.
source: In addition, ribbon number was significantly decreased (Figure 4L, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4L and Table 1.

claim: CtBP2 intensity was diminished in MafbCKO mutants at P3.
source: Although GluR2 immunofluorescence was not bright enough to assess PSD differentiation before P6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), CtBP2 intensity was also diminished at P3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D′), suggesting that SGN post-synaptic differentiation is impaired from the earliest stages.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D′.

claim: Mafb mutant SGNs fail to elaborate the specialized PSDs that are characteristic of auditory ribbon synapses.
source: Thus, Mafb mutant SGNs fail to elaborate the specialized PSDs that are characteristic of auditory ribbon synapses, apparently leading to defects in the development and anchoring of presynaptic ribbons in the IHCs.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations of PSD and ribbon defects in MafbCKO mutants.

claim: There was an approximately 50% reduction in the number of GluR2 puncta at P15 in MafbCKO mutants.
source: These reciprocal defects in early pre- and post-synaptic development resulted in a severe disruption in the mature pattern of synaptic connectivity, with an ∼50% reduction in the number of GluR2 puncta and an ∼30% reduction in ribbon number at P15 (Figure 4G–H′,K,L, Table 1)
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4K,L and Table 1.

claim: There was an approximately 30% reduction in ribbon number at P15 in MafbCKO mutants.
source: These reciprocal defects in early pre- and post-synaptic development resulted in a severe disruption in the mature pattern of synaptic connectivity, with an ∼50% reduction in the number of GluR2 puncta and an ∼30% reduction in ribbon number at P15 (Figure 4G–H′,K,L, Table 1)
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4K,L and Table 1.

claim: Many CtBP2-positive ribbons were not paired with a corresponding GluR2 spot at P15 in MafbCKO mutants.
source: Additionally, close examination of individual pre- and post-synaptic puncta showed that many CtBP2-positive ribbons were not paired with a corresponding GluR2 spot (Figure 4I,J).
evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 4I,J.

claim: The expression levels of GluR2 and PSD95 transcripts were similar between control and Mafb mutant SGNs.
source: This phenotype is not due to a general decrease in the transcription of PSD components, as the expression levels of GluR2 and PSD95 transcripts were similar between control and Mafb mutant SGNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The efferent innervation of the MafbCKO cochlea is normal.
source: In addition, the efferent innervation of the MafbCKO cochlea is normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mafb acts in SGN afferents to specify post-synaptic differentiation of ribbon synapses.
source: Thus, we conclude that Mafb acts in SGN afferents to specify post-synaptic differentiation of ribbon synapses.
evidence: Inferred from cell-type specific deletion of Mafb and resulting synaptic phenotypes.

claim: MafbCKO mice showed dampened ABR waveforms and elevated auditory thresholds.
source: In contrast, MafbCKO mice showed dampened ABR waveforms and elevated auditory thresholds, with thresholds increased ∼10 dB SPL across stimuli of all frequencies (Figure 5A,B,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ABR recordings shown in Figure 5A,B,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Thresholds of MafbCKO mice were significantly higher for all frequencies measured except the lowest and highest frequencies.
source: Thresholds of MafbCKO mice were significantly higher for all frequencies measured except the lowest and highest frequencies, since sensitivity is already reduced in these regions of control cochleae (Figure 5B) (p values: 5.6 kHz=0.125, 8 kHz=0.044, 11.3 kHz=0.043, 16 kHz=0.031, 22.6 kHz=0.038, 32 kHz=0.047, 45.2 kHz=0.140; n = 16 controls and 16 mutants).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of ABR threshold data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DPOAE levels were not significantly different in MafbCKO vs control mice.
source: DPOAE levels were not significantly different in MafbCKO vs control mice, regardless of the frequency and intensity of the stimulus used (Figure 5C), indicating that hair cell function is largely normal.
evidence: Supported by DPOAE measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ABR threshold elevation in MafbCKO mice is mainly caused by the reduced activation of SGNs by sound stimuli.
source: Hence, the ABR threshold elevation is mainly caused by the reduced activation of SGNs by sound stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from normal DPOAEs but elevated ABR thresholds.

claim: Wave I was delayed in MafbCKO mice, with increased latency in mutants exposed to a 16 kHz pure tone.
source: In MafbCKO mice, Wave I was delayed, with increased latency in mutants exposed to a 16 kHz pure tone (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by ABR wave I latency analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The amplitude of Wave I was significantly diminished in MafbCKO mice in response to stimuli across frequencies and intensities.
source: More strikingly, the amplitude was significantly diminished in response to stimuli across frequencies and intensities (Figure 5D,F,G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ABR wave I amplitude analysis shown in Figure 5D,F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The response to a 16 kHz, 80 dB stimulus was 35% smaller in MafbCKO mutants than in controls.
source: For instance, the response to a 16 kHz, 80 dB stimulus was 35% smaller in mutants than in controls.
evidence: Calculated from ABR wave I amplitude data.

claim: Loss of Mafb prevents the development of normal acoustic responsiveness, with effects along the length of the cochlea.
source: Hence, loss of Mafb prevents the development of normal acoustic responsiveness, with effects along the length of the cochlea.
evidence: Inferred from ABR defects across multiple frequencies.

claim: Maximum peak outward current amplitudes were not significantly different between MafbCKO mutants and littermate controls.
source: Maximum peak outward current amplitudes were not significantly different between MafbCKO mutants and littermate controls (MafbCKO: 4.1 ± 1.3 nA, n = 11; control: 4.4 ± 0.8 nA, n = 10)
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recordings from P3 SGNs.

claim: There was no significant difference in the current–voltage relationships between MafbCKO mutants and controls.
source: and there was no significant difference in the current–voltage relationships (Figure 6B, lower left panel).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No significant difference was found in INa between MafbCKO mutants and controls.
source: Again, no significant difference was found in INa (Figure 6B, lower right panel) (MafbCKO:−1.2 ± 1.5 nA, n = 7; controls: −2.1 ± 0.9 nA, n = 5).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Depolarizing current injections above 30 pA evoked action potentials in MafbCKO SGNs.
source: Depolarizing current injections above 30 pA evoked action potentials (APs) in MafbCKO SGNs (Figure 6C), suggesting that the AP firing machinery was not compromised.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Quantitative analyses of AP parameters indicated no significant difference between MafbCKO and control littermates.
source: Quantitative analyses of AP parameters, such as resting membrane potential, AP threshold, and AP latency, indicated no significant difference between MafbCKO and control littermates (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings and analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Intrinsic membrane and firing properties were unaltered in postnatal MafbCKO SGNs.
source: In summary, our results indicate that intrinsic membrane and firing properties were unaltered in postnatal MafbCKO SGNs.
evidence: Inferred from multiple electrophysiological measurements showing no differences.

claim: The elevated ABR threshold and reduced eighth nerve synchronization is a direct consequence of the IHC-SGN synapse defect.
source: We therefore propose that the elevated ABR threshold and reduced eighth nerve synchronization (Figure 5) is a direct consequence of the IHC-SGN synapse defect (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from normal SGN firing properties but abnormal synapses and ABRs.

claim: The emergence of normal SGN firing properties seems to be independent of Mafb.
source: Moreover, the emergence of normal SGN firing properties seems to be independent of Mafb.
evidence: Inferred from normal electrophysiological properties in MafbCKO SGNs.

claim: In MafbCE mice, Mafb protein was present in SGNs by E12.5.
source: In these mice, Mafb protein was present in SGNs by E12.5, at least 3 days earlier than the expression of endogenous Mafb protein in controls (Figure 7B–C′).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B-C′.

claim: Overexpression of Mafb had no gross effect on cochlear wiring.
source: Overexpression of Mafb had no gross effect on cochlear wiring (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by neurofilament staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: AMPA receptors clustered earlier in SGN terminals in MafbCE mice.
source: However, AMPA receptors clustered earlier in SGN terminals, with multiple patches of GluR2 staining covering the entire basal pole of the IHCs (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: There was a dramatic increase of GluR2 staining intensity in MafbCE afferent terminals at P6.
source: Quantification confirmed a dramatic increase of GluR2 staining intensity in MafbCE afferent terminals (Figure 7F) (p=0.033)
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Similar effects were observed for PSD95 in MafbCE mice.
source: with similar effects observed for a second PSD marker, PSD95 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Increased expression of Mafb enhanced post-synaptic differentiation in SGNs.
source: Hence, increased expression of Mafb enhanced post-synaptic differentiation in SGNs.
evidence: Inferred from increased GluR2 and PSD95 clustering in MafbCE mice.

claim: CtBP2-positive spots were noticeably more confined to the basal pole of the IHCs in P6 MafbCE mice.
source: In MafbCE mice, this process occurred earlier and CtBP2-positive spots were noticeably more confined to the basal pole of the IHCs (Figure 7D′,E′).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D′,E′.

claim: The nearest-neighbor distance of ribbons in P6 MafbCE mice was significantly shorter than in controls.
source: Indeed, the nearest-neighbor distance of ribbons in P6 MafbCE mice was significantly shorter (1.83 ± 0.03 µm, n = 428 ribbons) than in controls (2.06 ± 0.04 µm, n = 407 ribbons) (p<0.0001) (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by quantification of ribbon distribution shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Overexpression of Mafb caused synapses to develop earlier.
source: Hence, overexpression of Mafb caused synapses to develop earlier, as evidenced by increased accumulation of PSD components in SGN terminals and precocious basolateral localization of pre-synaptic ribbons in the hair cells.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations of accelerated synaptic development in MafbCE mice.

claim: The acceleration in synapse development in MafbCE mice did not cause any increase in the number of ribbons at P15.
source: Notably, this acceleration in synapse development did not cause any increase in the number of ribbons (Figure 7D′,E′,G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E′,F′, and Table 1) or GluR2-positive puncta (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E,F, and Table 1) at P15.
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E′,F′, and Table 1.

claim: Ribbon distribution was unchanged in P15 MafbCE mice compared to controls.
source: Ribbon distribution was also unchanged in P15 MafbCE mice compared to controls (p=0.63) (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The pruning and refinement of synapses appear to be controlled by an independent pathway that is unaffected by the overexpression of Mafb.
source: Thus, the pruning and refinement of synapses appear to be controlled by an independent pathway that is unaffected by the overexpression of Mafb.
evidence: Inferred from normal synapse numbers at P15 despite accelerated development.

claim: MafbCE SGNs exhibited normal firing properties.
source: Electrophysiological studies further confirmed that early and increased expression of Mafb does not seem to have adverse effects on SGN maturation. MafbCE SGNs exhibited normal firing properties (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: The majority (>80%) of MafbCE mice die at approximately 3 weeks of age due to unknown causes.
source: Unfortunately, the majority (>80%) of MafbCE mice die at ∼3 weeks of age due to unknown causes, so it was not possible to test whether hearing develops normally in these animals.
evidence: Observation of lethality in MafbCE mice.

claim: Expression of Mafb is sufficient to initiate synapse development, without disrupting synaptic pruning or other aspects of SGN function.
source: Nevertheless, our findings suggest that expression of Mafb is sufficient to initiate synapse development, without disrupting synaptic pruning or other aspects of SGN function.
evidence: Inferred from accelerated synapse development, normal pruning, and normal electrophysiology in MafbCE mice.

claim: In Gata3CKO mutants, Mafb protein levels were strongly reduced.
source: In Gata3CKO mutants, Mafb protein levels were strongly reduced (Figure 8B′).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8B′.

claim: The number of GluR2 and CtBP2 puncta was significantly decreased in P15 Gata3CKO mutants.
source: Consistent with this loss of Mafb, the number of GluR2 and CtBP2 puncta was significantly decreased in P15 Gata3CKO mutants (Figure 8E,E′,G and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 8E,E′,G and Table 1.

claim: Synaptic loss in Gata3CKO was more severe than what occurs in MafbCKO animals.
source: Synaptic loss in Gata3CKO (Figure 8G) was more severe than what occurs in MafbCKO animals (Figure 4K,L), which fits with Gata3's earlier and broader effects on SGN neurite outgrowth, axon guidance, and survival (Appler et al., 2013; Duncan and Fritzsch, 2013; Luo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by comparison of quantification data and cited literature on Gata3 functions.

claim: In Gata3CKO;MafbCE animals, Mafb protein was present in SGN nuclei, despite the absence of Gata3.
source: In Bhlhe22Cre/+;Gata3flox/tauLacZ;ROSA26CAG-lsl-Mafb animals (i.e., Gata3CKO;MafbCE), Mafb protein was present in SGN nuclei, despite the absence of Gata3 (Figure 8C,C′).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8C,C′.

claim: Restoration of Mafb was sufficient to improve the synaptic defect seen in Gata3CKO mutants.
source: Strikingly, this restoration of Mafb was sufficient to improve the synaptic defect seen in Gata3CKO mutants (compare Figure 8F,F′ to Figure 8E,E′), with an ∼80% increase in GluR2 puncta and an ∼50% increase in ribbon number in Gata3CKO;MafbCE mice when compared to Gata3CKO littermates (Figure 8G, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 8G and Table 1.

claim: Synapses could be rescued by resupplying Mafb to Gata3CKO mice made using the Neurog1-Cre line.
source: Synapses could also be rescued by resupplying Mafb to Gata3CKO mice made using the Neurog1-Cre line (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating that the effect is SGN-autonomous.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gata3 and Mafb are key players in a transcriptional cascade that guides SGN development and ensures the emergence of the cell-type specific features that are critical for the sense of hearing.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that Gata3 and Mafb are key players in a transcriptional cascade that guides SGN development and ensures the emergence of the cell-type specific features that are critical for the sense of hearing.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis experiments showing Gata3 regulates Mafb and Mafb rescues Gata3 mutant synaptic phenotype.

claim: Mafb plays a highly specific role, with dramatic effects on post-synaptic differentiation in the absence of any other obvious changes in SGN function.
source: Our results indicate that Mafb plays a highly specific role, with dramatic effects on post-synaptic differentiation in the absence of any other obvious changes in SGN function.
evidence: Inferred from synaptic defects without changes in SGN survival, targeting, or electrophysiology.

claim: Mafb was capable of restoring synapses even in the Gata3 mutant background, where SGN development is severely disrupted.
source: Indeed, Mafb was capable of restoring synapses even in the Gata3 mutant background, where SGN development is severely disrupted.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Mafb acts downstream of Gata3 to ensure formation of the specialized ribbon synapses that mediate the sense of hearing.
source: In this study, we showed that the emergence of cell-type specific features of synapse development can be controlled by late acting lineage-specific transcription factors, with Mafb acting downstream of Gata3 to ensure formation of the specialized ribbon synapses that mediate the sense of hearing.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis and rescue experiments.

claim: Mafb is a potent regulator of SGN terminal differentiation that functions within a broader Gata3 transcriptional network.
source: These findings establish Mafb as a potent regulator of SGN terminal differentiation that functions within a broader Gata3 transcriptional network, offering a potent molecular entry point for designing new treatments for age-related and noise-induced hearing loss.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental results showing Mafb's role in synapse development within Gata3 pathway.

claim: Gata3 is required for Mafb expression in SGNs.
source: Our findings add Mafb as a critical player downstream to Gata3: Gata3 is required for Mafb expression
evidence: Supported by loss of Mafb in Gata3CKO mutants.

claim: Mafb is sufficient to rescue synapses in Gata3CKO mutants.
source: and Mafb is sufficient to rescue synapses in Gata3CKO mutants.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments in Gata3CKO;MafbCE mice.

claim: Mafb provides a new example of a transcription factor that can direct post-synaptic differentiation, apparently in a cell-type specific manner.
source: Hence, Mafb provides a new example of a transcription factor that can direct post-synaptic differentiation, apparently in a cell-type specific manner.
evidence: Inferred from Mafb's specific effects on PSD development in SGNs.

claim: MafA and c-Maf are highly expressed in SGNs.
source: MafA and c-Maf are also highly expressed in SGNs (Lu et al., 2011 and W-MY and LVG, unpublished observation)
evidence: Supported by cited microarray data and unpublished observations.

claim: MafA and c-Maf have been shown to play important roles in the terminal differentiation of neurons in the dorsal root ganglia.
source: and both have been shown to play important roles in the terminal differentiation of neurons in the dorsal root ganglia (Bourane et al., 2009; Wende et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: There may be a Maf code for SGN terminal differentiation, with each factor directing a different feature required for mature function.
source: Thus, there may be a Maf code for SGN terminal differentiation, with each factor directing a different feature required for mature function.
evidence: Speculative inference based on expression of multiple Maf factors in SGNs and their known roles in other neurons.

claim: Mafb is not expressed until late in differentiation, just a day before functional synapses can first be detected.
source: Consistent with this definition, Mafb is not expressed until late in differentiation, just a day before functional synapses can first be detected (Marrs and Spirou, 2012)
evidence: Supported by temporal expression data and cited literature on synapse development.

claim: Mafb may activate expression of terminal effectors that drive synapse formation.
source: suggesting that Mafb may activate expression of terminal effectors that drive synapse formation.
evidence: Inferred from timing of Mafb expression and its effects on synapse development.

claim: Mafb is both necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of a key feature of mature SGN function, that is the ability to receive information from IHCs.
source: Additionally, Mafb is both necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of a key feature of mature SGN function, that is the ability to receive information from IHCs.
evidence: Inferred from loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments showing effects on PSD development.

claim: Mafb's persistent expression in adults fulfills an important criterion for terminal selectors.
source: Whether Mafb plays an ongoing role in SGNs remains to be determined, but its persistent expression in adults fulfills another important criterion.
evidence: Supported by expression data showing Mafb in adult SGNs.

claim: The absence of Mafb from vestibular ganglion neurons suggests that different sets of transcription factors may act in SGNs and VGNs to control post-synaptic differentiation.
source: Similarly, the absence of Mafb from vestibular ganglion neurons, which also form ribbon synapses, suggests that different sets of transcription factors may act in SGNs and VGNs to control post-synaptic differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from SGN-specific expression of Mafb despite both SGNs and VGNs forming ribbon synapses.

claim: Mafb is expressed by a handful of other neuronal subtypes and could play a similar role in the emergence of their cell-type specific properties.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that Mafb's effects might extend to other neuronal populations. Indeed, Mafb is expressed by a handful of other neuronal subtypes and could play a similar role in the emergence of their cell-type specific properties, including but not limited to synaptic differentiation.
evidence: Speculative inference based on Mafb expression in other neurons.

claim: Mafb is expressed in cochlear nucleus bushy cells.
source: For instance, in addition to being expressed in SGNs, Mafb is also expressed in cochlear nucleus bushy cells (Saul et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Mafb defines subsets of cortical interneurons.
source: Similarly, Mafb defines subsets of cortical interneurons (Wang et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Mafb defines a subpopulation of rhythmogenic neurons within the pre-Bötzinger complex.
source: and a subpopulation of rhythmogenic neurons within the pre-Bötzinger complex (Blanchi et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: One of the earliest effects of acoustic overexposure is the loss of synapses followed by withdrawal of SGN terminals.
source: One of the earliest effects of acoustic overexposure is the loss of synapses followed by withdrawal of SGN terminals.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: SGNs undergo a long slow degeneration after acoustic overexposure, ultimately resulting in significant hearing loss long after the original injury.
source: The SGNs subsequently undergo a long slow degeneration, ultimately resulting in significant hearing loss long after the original injury (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Stimulation of Mafb might be sufficient to encourage damaged neurons to re-establish connections with IHCs.
source: Our results suggest that stimulation of Mafb might be sufficient to encourage damaged neurons to re-establish connections with IHCs.
evidence: Speculative inference based on Mafb's role in synapse formation.

claim: The specificity of Mafb's effects implies that synapses could be restored without inadvertently interfering with other aspects of SGN function.
source: Moreover, the specificity of Mafb's effects implies that synapses could be restored without inadvertently interfering with other aspects of SGN function.
evidence: Inferred from Mafb's specific effects on synapses without affecting other SGN properties.

claim: Mafb is still present in the adult cochlea, largely sequestered in the cytoplasm.
source: Importantly, we find that Mafb is still present in the adult cochlea (data not shown), largely sequestered in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Stated observation of Mafb localization in adults.

claim: Drugs that enhance translocation of Mafb into the nucleus might offer a new treatment for deafness.
source: Ultimately, drugs that enhance translocation of Mafb into the nucleus might offer a new treatment for deafness.
evidence: Speculative inference based on Mafb's role and cytoplasmic localization in adults.

claim: Functional dopaminergic and spinal motor neurons can be directly generated from somatic cells by ectopic expression of lineage specific transcription factors.
source: Indeed, recent studies have shown that functional dopaminergic and spinal motor neurons can be directly generated from somatic cells by ectopic expression of lineage specific transcription factors (Caiazzo et al., 2011; Son et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: SGN neurogenesis occurs along a base to apex gradient, with most SGNs exiting the cell cycle by E12.5.
source: SGN neurogenesis occurs along a base to apex gradient, with most SGNs exiting the cell cycle by E12.5 and extending projections to reach the organ of Corti by E15.5 (Matei et al., 2005; Koundakjian et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: SGNs extend projections to reach the organ of Corti by E15.5.
source: SGN neurogenesis occurs along a base to apex gradient, with most SGNs exiting the cell cycle by E12.5 and extending projections to reach the organ of Corti by E15.5 (Matei et al., 2005; Koundakjian et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Ribbon synapses begin to develop perinatally in mice.
source: In mice, ribbon synapses begin to develop perinatally (Sobkowicz et al., 1982; Nemzou et al., 2006; Sendin et al., 2007; Marrs and Spirou, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Presynaptic ribbons are initially distributed throughout the IHC cytoplasm and then gradually localize to the basolateral surface to form an immature synapse.
source: Presynaptic ribbons are initially distributed throughout the IHC cytoplasm and then gradually localize to the basolateral surface to form an immature synapse, with clustered ribbons in large active zones (Sobkowicz et al., 1982; Sendin et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: SGN neurites reach IHCs and begin to elaborate post-synaptic terminals, characterized by increased clustering of GluR2/R3 AMPA receptors in the nascent PSD.
source: In parallel, SGN neurites reach IHCs and begin to elaborate post-synaptic terminals, characterized by increased clustering of GluR2/R3 AMPA receptors in the nascent PSD (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Ribbon number peaks at the end of the first postnatal week.
source: Ribbon number peaks at the end of the first postnatal week, followed by a period of pruning and refinement.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: By the onset of hearing (P12 in mice), ribbon number has declined to adult levels.
source: By the onset of hearing (postnatal day 12 [P12] in mice), ribbon number has declined to adult levels and each ribbon is anchored opposite a specialized large, well-defined PSD in the SGN terminal (Sobkowicz et al., 1982; Nemzou et al., 2006; Sendin et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: In mature animals, the size of the PSD correlates with the size and position of the ribbon.
source: In mature animals, the size of the PSD correlates with the size and position of the ribbon (Liberman et al., 2011), indicating that pre- and post-synaptic development must be tightly coordinated.
evidence: Supported by cited literature and inference about coordination.

claim: Without SGN afferent terminals, ribbon development in IHCs is impaired.
source: Indeed, without SGN afferent terminals, ribbon development in IHCs is impaired (Sobkowicz et al., 1986)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Afferent terminals are not stabilized in mutants lacking normal ribbons.
source: and conversely, afferent terminals are not stabilized in mutants lacking normal ribbons (Sheets et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Gata3 is expressed in SGNs as soon as they can be identified.
source: Efforts to understand how SGNs acquire their auditory-specific features have established an important role for the Gata3 transcription factor, which is expressed in SGNs as soon as they can be identified (Lawoko-Kerali et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Gata3 is maintained throughout SGN differentiation.
source: and then maintained throughout differentiation (Appler et al., 2013; Duncan and Fritzsch, 2013; Luo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Upon deletion of Gata3, cochlear wiring is severely disrupted.
source: Upon deletion of Gata3, cochlear wiring is severely disrupted and SGNs fail to express a cohort of auditory-specific genes (Appler et al., 2013; Duncan and Fritzsch, 2013)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: SGNs fail to express a cohort of auditory-specific genes upon deletion of Gata3.
source: Upon deletion of Gata3, cochlear wiring is severely disrupted and SGNs fail to express a cohort of auditory-specific genes (Appler et al., 2013; Duncan and Fritzsch, 2013)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Mafb belongs to the family of large Maf factors.
source: Mafb belongs to the family of large Maf factors, which activate cell-type specific programs of gene expression essential for terminal differentiation of a wide variety of cell types, including pancreatic β cells, kidney podocytes, and macrophages (Moriguchi et al., 2006; Kataoka, 2007; Hang and Stein, 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Large Maf factors activate cell-type specific programs of gene expression essential for terminal differentiation of a wide variety of cell types.
source: Mafb belongs to the family of large Maf factors, which activate cell-type specific programs of gene expression essential for terminal differentiation of a wide variety of cell types, including pancreatic β cells, kidney podocytes, and macrophages (Moriguchi et al., 2006; Kataoka, 2007; Hang and Stein, 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Mafb was first identified as the genetic cause of the kreisler mutation (kr) in mice.
source: Mafb was first identified as the genetic cause of the kreisler mutation (kr) in mice (Cordes and Barsh, 1994).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: In kreisler mutants, rhombomeres 5 and 6 are not properly specified.
source: In kr mutants, rhombomeres 5 and 6 are not properly specified, and the otic vesicle, which develops adjacent to these structures, fails to acquire its normal morphology.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about kreisler mutants.

claim: The otic vesicle fails to acquire its normal morphology in kreisler mutants.
source: In kr mutants, rhombomeres 5 and 6 are not properly specified, and the otic vesicle, which develops adjacent to these structures, fails to acquire its normal morphology.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about kreisler mutants.

claim: Mafb is required in the pre-Bötzinger complex in the hindbrain.
source: Although its function in the nervous system remains unclear, Mafb is also required in the pre-Bötzinger complex in the hindbrain (Blanchi et al., 2003):
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Respiratory circuits are unable to mediate normal breathing in Mafb mutants, which die from central apnea at birth.
source: respiratory circuits are unable to mediate normal breathing in Mafb mutants, which die from central apnea at birth.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about Mafb mutants.

claim: SGNs encode the frequency, intensity, and timing of all acoustic stimuli.
source: As the sole link between IHCs and the brain, SGNs encode the frequency, intensity, and timing of all acoustic stimuli and communicate this information rapidly and faithfully to the brain (Appler and Goodrich, 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: SGNs receive information from IHCs via ribbon synapses that are specialized for signaling with high temporal precision.
source: To achieve the necessary speed, SGNs receive information from IHCs via ribbon synapses that are specialized for signaling with high temporal precision (Khimich et al., 2005; Glowatzki et al., 2008; Buran et al., 2010; Safieddine et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Ribbon synapses contain an electron-dense multi-protein ribbon structure, which tethers a large pool of readily releasable vesicles.
source: Unlike conventional synapses, ribbon synapses contain an electron-dense multi-protein ribbon structure, which tethers a large pool of readily releasable vesicles (Sterling and Matthews, 2005; Goutman and Glowatzki, 2007; Frank et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Ribbon synapses enable fast and sustained release of glutamate from the IHCs.
source: thereby enabling fast and sustained release of glutamate from the IHCs (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: SGNs respond with remarkable speed due to a large postsynaptic density containing abundant clusters of AMPA-type receptors.
source: Likewise, SGNs respond with remarkable speed due to a large postsynaptic density (PSD) containing abundant clusters of AMPA-type receptors (Matsubara et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Auditory synaptopathies underlie several forms of hearing loss.
source: Indeed, auditory synaptopathies underlie several forms of hearing loss (Moser et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Ribbon synapses are particularly vulnerable to acoustic overexposure.
source: and ribbon synapses are particularly vulnerable to acoustic overexposure (Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.
